period.text: The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves were cut into the rock in about the 2nd–1st century BCE.
period.note: Percy Brown: the Orissan caves were cut within about 150 years before the Common Era; he reads a mean date of about 160 BCE from the Hathigumpha inscription.

design_change.text: These are not temples. They are monasteries: rooms cut into the rock for monks. The local name for them is gumpha (cave).

dynasty.text: The Hathigumpha inscription tells of King Kharavela, ruler of Kalinga. He was a Jain, and he seems to have taken a special interest in the monks who lived in these hills.
dynasty.note: Percy Brown reads the Hathigumpha inscription this way. He writes that Kharavela 'was by religion a Jain, and appears to have been personally interested in the priestly community who had selected these hills as a place of retreat.'

temples.name: Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves (incl. Rani Gumpha, Hathi Gumpha)

period.text: Experts still argue about the age of the earliest Bhubaneswar temples. One careful guess puts them between about 750 and 900 CE. Another says some are even older.
period.note: Panigrahi places the Parasuramesvara group in the Shailodbhava period, which by his tentative chronology ended in the second half of the 8th century CE. Brown dates Parasuramesvara towards the end of the 8th century CE and his Early period to c. 750–900 CE.

design_change.text: A basic Odisha temple has two buildings: the deul (shrine tower) and the jagamohana (front hall). Parasuramesvara has both. Its tower is still simple, short, sturdy and heavy, like a first draft.
design_change.note: Percy Brown: two buildings 'combined constitute the essentials of the Orissan temple type'; he calls the Parasuramesvara tower's shape 'definitely rudimentary' and the temple itself 'inclined to be heavy and crude.'

design_change.text: The Vaital Deul has a rounded, vaulted roof, like a barrel. Experts think this shape carries on from the roofs of old Buddhist chaitya (prayer) halls.
design_change.note: Percy Brown saw this roof as a survival of the Buddhist chaitya-hall roof: 'its unmistakable vaulted roof occasionally survives in the Hindu temple, as for instance in ... the singularly interesting Vaital Deul.'

dynasty.text: This was the time of the Shailodbhava kings, then the Bhauma-Kara kings. No one knows for certain which king built which temple here.
dynasty.note: K. C. Panigrahi: 'we do not know whether any of the Sailodbhava rulers was a builder of any of the temples here'; of the Bhauma-Karas, 'there is not a single tradition ... which connects any of the known rulers of the dynasty with any of its numerous existing monuments.'

period.text: From about 900 to 1100 CE, the Odisha style reached its early prime: its first high point.
period.note: Percy Brown calls this his 'Middle Period', dating it 'cir. 900 to 1100 A.D.' and describing it as 'the movement at its early maturity or prime.'

design_change.text: Mukteshvara is a 'miniature gem' — highly finished, decorated with carved patterns, and reached through a torana (arched gateway). It is one of the few Odisha temples with carvings inside too.
design_change.note: Percy Brown: Mukteshvara 'is a miniature gem of architecture ... highly finished structure, ornamented with fascinating carved patterns ... approached by an arched gateway, or torana', and 'one of the few temples of the Orissan group which has sculptured decoration in its interior.'

design_change.text: Some experts think that art and building styles from the upper Mahanadi valley (old Kosala) travelled to Utkala (Odisha) — and helped start a revival of art there.
design_change.note: K. C. Panigrahi argues this: 'we have shown how the art and architecture of the Upper Mahanadi Valley ... travelled to Utkala to initiate a revival of artistic conceptions.'

dynasty.text: This was the age of the Somavamshi (Kesari) kings. Their dynasty was founded by King Janamejaya.
dynasty.note: K. C. Panigrahi: 'it was Janamejaya who founded the Somavamsi or Kesari dynasty of Kosala and Utkala.'

period.text: The Lingaraja temple is dated to about 1000 CE. The present Jagannath temple at Puri is dated to about 1100 CE.
period.note: Percy Brown: Lingaraja c. 1000 CE; Jagannath about 1100 CE, 'not consecrated until' 1118 CE, and linked to 'Chora Ganga, the conqueror of Kalinga in 1030'. K. C. Panigrahi: Chodaganga's rule in Odisha is shown by a Lingaraja inscription of 1114 CE. Dates rest on style and later records.

design_change.text: The fully developed temple had four buildings in a line. In front of the jagamohana (front hall) came the natamandira (dance hall), then the bhogamandapa (hall of offerings). At Lingaraja these two halls were added later, probably a century or more after the rest.
At Lingaraja the tower walls rise straight at first, then curve inward more and more toward the top. At Puri, the top of this curve is given a more graceful line.
design_change.note: Percy Brown, on the shoulder curve at Puri: 'the overhang of the shoulder, which in this instance has been reduced to a more graceful line, giving its profile additional refinement and balance.'

dynasty.text: Somavamshi kings raised the greatest Shiva temple at Bhubaneswar. Later, the Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga conquered Utkala (Odisha).
dynasty.note: K. C. Panigrahi: 'the kings of the dynasty were instrumental in raising the greatest Saiva temple at Bhubaneswar besides a number of smaller ones'; 'The direct connexion of the Gangas with Utkala or Orissa began with its conquest by Anantavarman Chodagangadeva.'

period.text: The Sun Temple at Konark was built in the 13th century CE, around the middle of that century.

design_change.text: Konark's parts were all planned together as one design, unlike the separate buildings of Lingaraja and Jagannath. The whole temple is shaped like the chariot of Surya, the Sun god, with wheels and seven horses.
design_change.note: Percy Brown: Konark is 'a reasoned and systematic co-ordination of its parts into an architectural unity', 'fashioned like a ratha or wheeled car being whirled along by the seven horses of the sun.' Seven horses follows Brown; the short UNESCO summary page says six.

design_change.text: Konark's main tower has fallen, and only its foundations remain. The jagamohana (front hall) is the part that still stands fairly intact.

period.text: The Suryavamshi (Gajapati) kings ruled Odisha from the 15th century CE. Their power was already fading by the early 16th century CE, under King Prataparudra.
period.note: Panigrahi gives Kapilendra's accession as 1435 CE on one page and his reign as 1433–1467 CE on another.

design_change.text: The great age of temple building ended with the Gangas, though some notable temples were still built. The architectural style changed little, but sculpture declined.
design_change.note: K. C. Panigrahi: 'After the Gangas, the glorious period of temple-building activities in Orissa was over, but the spirit lingered on ... which also witnessed the erection of some notable temples'; 'the dynastic change did not result in any great change in architectural style, but in sculpture a definite set-back is to be perceived.'

design_change.text: The Kapilesvara temple in Bhubaneswar may belong to this period, but no one is sure. Like the great Ganga temples, it has three halls in front of its shrine.
design_change.note: Panigrahi dates it by style only. He says it 'seems to have belonged to this period' and 'appears to be the last notable monument' at Bhubaneswar. He says it stands on the site of an earlier temple.

dynasty.text: The Suryavamshi (Gajapati) dynasty was founded by Kapilendra, once a Ganga officer. It produced two more able rulers, Purushottama and Prataparudra.
